title: Main Ideas & Note-Taking
keyIdea: The main idea of a paragraph is what every sentence in it tells about. Key details back up the main idea. A summary joins the main ideas of several paragraphs in a few short sentences, in your own words. Notes are key words from the text, recorded in a table, in numbered steps or in a spider diagram, so you can find them again.

kid: Every paragraph is about one big thing. That is its main idea. Ask: what do all the sentences tell about? In a paragraph about what hedgehogs eat, each sentence tells about food. So the main idea is what hedgehogs eat.
Key details are the small facts that back up the main idea. A fact can be true and still not fit. “Hedgehogs can swim” is true. But it does not fit in a paragraph about food.
A summary is short. Take the main idea of each paragraph and say it in your own words. Leave out small details. Leave out what you think, too. Only say what the text says.

Notes are key words, not whole sentences. Put them where you can find them again. A table is good to compare things. Numbered steps are good for things in order. A spider diagram is good for facts about one thing.
adult: This lesson covers two linked reading skills. In England, upper key stage 2 pupils identify main ideas drawn from more than one paragraph and summarise them, and lower key stage 2 pupils retrieve and record information from non-fiction. In the US the match is Common Core RI.3.2, RI.4.2 and RI.5.2 (determine the main idea, explain how key details support it, and summarise the text).

Key terms for ages 7 to 10: topic, main idea, key details, supporting details, paragraph, summarise, summary, retrieve, record, notes, key words, table, numbered steps (sequence) and spider diagram (mind map). The topic is the subject in one or two words; the main idea is what the text says about that topic.

Common mistakes: giving the topic (“hedgehogs”) or one striking detail (“they walk 2 km”) instead of the main idea. Treating every true fact as a key detail. Writing a summary that is as long as the text, retells one paragraph only, or adds an opinion. Copying whole sentences as notes, which skips the thinking that makes notes useful.

In the lab your child reads a short hedgehog article. They drag the main idea of each paragraph into a box, tap the sentence that does not fit, and sort sentences into a summary or out of it. Then they record notes about bats in a table, bin the poor ones, and choose a table, steps or a spider diagram for three tasks. Every drag has a button twin.

familyTip: After reading any short article together, cover it and ask your child to say each paragraph's main idea in five words or fewer. Then write three key-word notes together on a sticky note, and check them against the text.

visual.caption: Main idea or key detail? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: What hedgehogs eat and how they find it
How spines keep a hedgehog safe
They hibernate from November to March
They roll into a ball when scared

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find each paragraph's main idea, spot the sentence that does not fit, build a summary, file notes in a table and choose how to record.

practice.prompt: Every sentence in a paragraph tells about how owls hunt at night. What is its main idea?
practice.hint: Ask what all the sentences tell about, not just one of them.
practice.explain: The main idea is how owls hunt at night. “Owls” is only the topic, and big eyes is one detail.

practice.prompt: An article has {n} paragraphs. Your summary keeps one main idea from each paragraph. How many main ideas are in your summary?
practice.hint: One main idea for each paragraph, so count the paragraphs.
practice.explain: One main idea from each of {n} paragraphs gives {=n} main ideas in the summary.

practice.prompt: Which is the best note about what bats eat?
choices: They hunt moths, midges and other insects at night.
practice.hint: A note is key words from the text, not a whole sentence or what you think.
practice.explain: moths, midges, insects is the best note: just the key words. The long one is copied, and yucky is an opinion.

practice.prompt: Your notes table compares {a} animals. Each animal has a row with {b} facts in it. How many facts are in the table?
practice.hint: There are {a} rows and {b} facts in each row. Multiply.
practice.explain: {a} rows with {b} facts each makes {=a*b} facts in the table.

practice.prompt: You want to record how a seed grows into a plant. What is the best way?
practice.hint: A seed grows in an order: first, next, last.
practice.explain: Numbered steps are best, because a seed grows in order. A table is for comparing things side by side.

pool.prompt: A paragraph says frogs lay eggs in ponds, the eggs hatch into tadpoles, and tadpoles grow legs. What is its main idea?
choices: How a frog grows from an egg
pool.hint: Find the thing that every sentence tells about.
pool.explain: The main idea is how a frog grows from an egg. Frogs is the topic, and tadpoles grow legs is one detail.

pool.prompt: Main idea: how bees make honey. Which sentence is NOT a key detail?
choices: They store it in wax cells in the hive.
pool.hint: A key detail must tell about making honey.
pool.explain: Bees can sting is true, but it is not about making honey, so it is not a key detail here.

pool.prompt: Which sentence should NOT go in a summary of a text about rivers?
choices: I think rivers are the best place to play.
Rivers start high up and flow to the sea.
Rivers carry water, soil and stones.
pool.hint: A summary only says what the text says.
pool.explain: I think rivers are the best place to play is an opinion, so it does not go in a summary.

choices: The main ideas, short, in your own words
pool.hint: Think of the summary you built in the lab.
pool.explain: A good summary is the main ideas, short, in your own words. It leaves out small details.

pool.prompt: A text has {n} paragraphs. You write one short main-idea sentence for each. How many sentences is your summary?
pool.explain: One sentence for each of {n} paragraphs makes a summary of {=n} sentences.

pool.prompt: You read {n} pages and write {k} key-word notes on each page. How many notes do you write?
pool.hint: {k} notes for each of {n} pages. Multiply.
pool.explain: {n} pages with {k} notes on each makes {=n*k} notes.

pool.prompt: You want to compare what lions, zebras and elephants eat. How should you record it?
pool.hint: Which way puts things side by side?
pool.explain: A table is best, because it puts the three animals side by side so you can compare them.

pool.prompt: Why are notes key words and not whole sentences?
choices: They are quick to write and easy to find again
So nobody else can read them
pool.hint: Think about why you make notes at all.
pool.explain: Key words are quick to write and easy to find again. Copying whole sentences takes longer and skips the thinking.

pool.prompt: You jot down facts about sharks under the headings Body, Food and Home. What is this?
pool.hint: Facts about one thing, sorted under headings around it.
pool.explain: It is a spider diagram: facts about one thing, sorted under headings.
